title: Path traversal in GET /attachments lets any logged-in user read arbitrary server-readable files
description: GET /attachments (app.py:88-92) requires only a session user_id, then passes request.args['name'] unchanged into os.path.join(UPLOAD_DIR, name) and flask.send_file with no normalization or containment check. '../' segments leave uploads/ and an absolute name makes os.path.join discard UPLOAD_DIR. The sibling /avatars route uses send_from_directory (app.py:97), which is the contained variant. A verifier read Flask 3.1.3 helpers.send_file and Werkzeug 3.1.9 utils.send_file in a local uv cache and found no safe_join on this path, but the behavior was not observed running. Impact if confirmed: read of any file the server process can read, including notes.db (plaintext passwords, seed.py:13). Suggested fix: use send_from_directory(UPLOAD_DIR, name) or werkzeug.security.safe_join with abort(404) on None; regression cases ?name=../notes.db and an absolute path must both return 404.
claimed_root_cause: The user-controlled query parameter 'name' is joined onto UPLOAD_DIR and passed to send_file without containment or normalization.

trace.description: Route reachable by any client with a valid session cookie; current_user() at line 90 checks only that user_id exists.
name is read from the query string with no validation, allow-list, or basename stripping.
os.path.join(UPLOAD_DIR, name) does not contain the path: '../' segments escape and an absolute name replaces UPLOAD_DIR.
send_file opens and streams the resulting path; the library read by the verifier adds no containment on this call.

evidence.description: The only gate is current_user(), a session presence check with no ownership or role logic.
Unsanitized os.path.join(UPLOAD_DIR, name) is passed directly to send_file.
Contrast: /avatars uses send_from_directory, which applies safe_join; /attachments does not.
users table stores plaintext passwords in notes.db, one '../' from UPLOAD_DIR, a concrete traversal target.

blockers: No verified OS-enforced sandbox on this host, so no target code was run and no observed result exists.
Library behavior was read from a uv-cache copy of Flask 3.1.3 / Werkzeug 3.1.9 source, not observed running; that these are the versions that run this app is not established.
Process filesystem permissions and any front-end that normalizes '../' or rejects absolute names are not visible from source.

validation_plan.local: In a scratch copy of the repo, run seed.py to create notes.db and uploads/welcome.txt. From a separate script directory, run python -I with the already-installed Flask and use app.test_client() with no network. Control: GET /attachments?name=welcome.txt with no session expects 401; after POST /login as alice, expects 200 with the welcome text. Test: GET /attachments?name=../notes.db expects 200 with a body beginning 'SQLite format 3' if the bug is real, and GET with the absolute path of the copy's seed.py expects 200. Contrast: GET /avatars/..%2Fnotes.db expects 404. After applying send_from_directory, the two traversal requests must return 404.

title: Invoice endpoint lacks an ownership check: any logged-in user can read any invoice by id
description: GET /invoices/<int:invoice_id> calls current_user() at app.py:78 and discards the result, queries invoices by id alone (app.py:79-82), and returns id, owner_id, customer and amount_cents (app.py:85). From the seed data, alice (id 1) could request /invoices/2 and read bob's Globex invoice (seed.py:20). The verifier found no decorator, before_request hook, or role/tenant logic that binds ownership, and no sharing model that would make cross-user access intended. The path is plain application logic, so source establishes it; only the observed local result is missing. Suggested fix: user_id = current_user() and query 'WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?' with 404 on no match; regression case: alice requesting invoice 2 gets 404.
claimed_root_cause: get_invoice discards the authenticated user id returned by current_user() and selects the invoice by primary key alone, so there is no owner_id = session user predicate.

trace.description: Route reachable by any logged-in low-privilege user; invoice_id is attacker-chosen and cast to int by Flask.
current_user() aborts 401 only when no session user_id exists; its return value is discarded, so identity is never bound to the query.
Parameterized query with id as the only predicate (app.py:80-81) and no owner_id filter.
jsonify(dict(row)) returns the matched invoice, including owner_id, regardless of who owns it.

evidence.description: current_user() is called as a bare statement, unlike list_notes (app.py:58) and search_notes (app.py:69), which assign and use user_id.
The SQL selects from invoices WHERE id = ? with no owner_id condition.
Invoice 1 belongs to user 1 and invoice 2 to user 2, giving a cross-user test pair.

blockers: No verified OS-enforced sandbox on this host, so no target code was run and no bounded local reproduction was observed. Source review found no refuting control.

validation_plan.local: In a scratch copy, run seed.py, then use python -I with the already-installed Flask and app.test_client() (no network). POST /login as alice/alice-pw; GET /invoices/1 expects 200 with owner_id 1; GET /invoices/2 expects 200 with {id 2, owner_id 2, customer Globex, amount_cents 990000} if the bug is real, while a 403/404 would refute it. Control: an unauthenticated client GET /invoices/2 expects 401. After the owner-scoped query fix, alice requesting invoice 2 must return 404.

title: SQL injection in GET /notes/search: unparameterized q can escape the owner filter and read other tables
description: search_notes reads q (app.py:70) and interpolates it into a LIKE literal with an f-string (app.py:71), then runs it with no bound parameters (app.py:72) and returns rows as JSON (app.py:73). A quote in q can close the literal and remove the owner_id scope, and the two-column shape (id, title) admits a two-column UNION against other tables, including users (plaintext passwords, seed.py:13-16). user_id comes from the signed session and is not request-controlled here. sqlite3 execute() allows one statement, so impact is read access via OR/UNION, not stacked writes. Exact payload behavior was inferred from SQLite semantics and the seed schema, not observed. Suggested fix: bind both values, 'WHERE owner_id = ? AND title LIKE ?' with (user_id, f'%{q}%'); regression: q="' OR '1'='1" returns only the caller's rows.
claimed_root_cause: User-controlled q is concatenated into the SQL text by an f-string at app.py:71 instead of being passed as a bound parameter, so SQL syntax in q changes the query structure including the owner_id predicate.

trace.description: Reachable by any caller holding a valid session; current_user() at line 69 aborts only when user_id is missing.
q = request.args.get('q', '') takes the raw value with no validation, length limit, or escaping.
f-string builds the SQL with q inside a single-quoted LIKE literal, so a quote ends the literal and the rest of q parses as SQL.
db().execute(sql) runs the interpolated string with no parameters; rows are returned by jsonify at line 73.

evidence.description: q is interpolated inside LIKE '%...%', unlike the bound parameters at lines 47, 61-62 and 80-81.
The only control is current_user(), which does no input filtering.
Result rows are returned as JSON, so UNION-selected data would be directly visible.
users has id, username, password, which fits a two-column UNION against SELECT id, title.

blockers: No verified OS-enforced sandbox on this host, so target code was not run and no bounded local reproduction was performed.
Exact UNION/OR payload results (column count, type affinity, comment handling, JSON output) are inferred from SQLite semantics and the seed schema, not observed.

validation_plan.local: In a scratch copy, run seed.py to create a throwaway notes.db, then use python -I with the already-installed Flask and app.test_client() (no network). Log in as alice/alice-pw. Baseline: GET /notes/search?q=Alice returns only note 1. Scope bypass: q = "zzz%' OR owner_id=2 --" returns 'Bob secret plans' if the bug is real. UNION: q = "zzz%' UNION SELECT id, username||':'||password FROM users --" returns 'alice:alice-pw' and 'bob:bob-pw' if real. Repeat both after the bound-parameter fix; each must return an empty list. Do not run destructive payloads.

title: Hardcoded Flask session-signing key would allow forging a session cookie for any user_id
description: app.py:17 sets app.secret_key to a literal string, with no environment or config override (the only environment read is PORT at app.py:101). current_user() (app.py:36-40) accepts any session['user_id'] once Flask's signed cookie verifies, with no server-side session record or other credential. Anyone who can read the source could therefore sign a cookie for user_id 1 or 2 (seed.py:16) and pass every current_user() gate (/notes, /notes/search, /invoices/<id>, /attachments) without calling /login. The docstring (app.py:3-4) says demo-only and the bind is 127.0.0.1 (app.py:101); those are context, not mitigations. Flask's signing behavior was stated from general knowledge and not read from installed source by this verifier. Suggested fix: load the key from a per-deployment secret (fail startup if absent, at least 32 random bytes) and rotate the committed value; consider server-side sessions for revocation.
claimed_root_cause: The session-signing secret is a constant committed to source, so the cookie signature gives no authentication guarantee against anyone holding the code.

trace.description: The signing key is a literal in source with no override; an anonymous client holding the source knows it.
session.get('user_id') reads identity from the cookie once the signature verifies against the known key.
current_user() returns the cookie-chosen user_id with no further authentication.
The notes query runs with owner_id equal to the forged user_id, returning that user's notes.

evidence.description: app.secret_key is assigned a literal constant.
current_user() trusts session['user_id'] and only aborts 401 when it is absent.
The only environment read is PORT; the key is never overridden.

blockers: No verified OS-enforced sandbox on this host, so no code was run and no bounded local reproduction was observed.
Flask/itsdangerous SecureCookieSessionInterface behavior was not read from installed source by this verifier, so cookie acceptance is unverified.
Exploitation requires the attacker to know the key, i.e. read access to the source; who can read the repository is a deployment fact not determinable from source.

validation_plan.local: In a scratch copy, run seed.py, then with the already-installed Flask build a cookie in a separate script (a = Flask('x'); a.secret_key = <the literal from app.py:17>; c = a.session_interface.get_signing_serializer(a).dumps({'user_id': 2})). Using app.test_client() with no network and no prior login, send GET /notes with that cookie: HTTP 200 containing 'Bob secret plans' would confirm it. Control: a cookie signed with a different key must return 401.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner can confirm whether any running instance uses the committed value by checking its configured SECRET_KEY, or by rotating the key and confirming old cookies are rejected; no audit traffic should be sent to a deployment.
